summary: This document enhances real-time text (RFC 4103) for centralized conferences. A mixer can identify sources and interleave text from different participants quickly, using the Contributing Source list in RTP packets. A capability exchange uses an SDP attribute called rtt-mixer. It also covers formatting for endpoints that are not multiparty aware, and updates RFC 4103.

eli5.summary: In a group chat that types out live, you need to know who is typing. This document lets a central mixer label each person's live text so everyone sees who said what.

questions: how does rtp mixer identify text sources
what is the cps parameter in real-time text
subtitle: How a central mixer can label and interleave live typed text from many people in one RTP stream.

tldr.problem: The real-time text format of RFC 4103 has no way to say who a piece of text came from, and its redundancy scheme assumes one source, so a conference mixer cannot interleave text from several people quickly.
tldr.mechanism: The mixer sends each packet with text from exactly one source and names that source as the single member of the RTP CSRC list. Support is negotiated with a new SDP media attribute, rtt-mixer, and a fallback inserts text labels for endpoints that are not multiparty aware.
tldr.outcome: Multiparty-aware endpoints can show each participant's text separately and in near real time. The RFC updates RFC 4103.

today: RFC 9071 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 4103. No later RFC is recorded as obsoleting or updating it.

sections.title: The Problem with Multiparty Real-Time Text
sections.content:
Real-time text (RTT) is text sent instantly as it is typed, so recipients can read it while it is being written. RFC 4103 carries it over RTP using the text/t140 format, with an optional text/red redundancy format for robustness.

RFC 4103's redundancy header has no source indicator for the redundant parts, so they must come from the same source as the new text. The recommended transmission is one new and two redundant generations of text (T140blocks) per packet, sent every 300 ms for two-party use. A mixer in a conference therefore cannot quickly take turns between people.

The motivating case is emergency calls. An agent often has to transfer the call to a specialized agent but must stay on it to check the transfer worked. The RFC also states a requirement from T.140 that each participant's text be clearly readable and show its source and relative timing, and a requirement that mixing add no disruptive delay.
sections.eli5: The old way assumes only two people are typing. With a group, the helper in the middle could not tell the receiver whose words were whose without slowing things down.

sections.title: Two Methods and the Alternatives Considered
sections.content:
The RFC specifies two methods. The main one is the RTP-mixer method for multiparty-aware endpoints: it reuses the existing formats and indicates the source in the CSRC field. The fallback is mixing for multiparty-unaware endpoints, which works at the presentation level by inserting readable labels into the text.

Three other approaches were considered. Multiple RTP streams, one per participant, could use the same packet format and could even allow end-to-end encryption through a Selective Forwarding Middlebox. However, it needs multi-stream RTP support that is lacking in some implementations, so it is mentioned only as an option for further study. A new media subtype carrying up to 15 sources per packet would perform well but would need new standardization and releases, so it was not chosen. The WebRTC data channel approach of RFC 8865 is mentioned only for gateways.

The RTP-mixer method gives good performance with ten participants typing at the same time. More than that causes noticeable jerkiness, which the RFC considers rare because simultaneous typing by more than two people is expected to be very rare.
sections.eli5: They looked at a few ways to do this. They picked the one that works with the equipment people already have, and kept a simpler backup plan for old devices.

sections.title: Negotiating with the rtt-mixer Attribute
sections.content:
Capability is announced in SDP with a media attribute: a=rtt-mixer. A party willing to use the method SHALL include it in the text media section of its offer. The answerer SHALL include it in the answer if it is willing too, and MUST NOT include it if the offer did not.

Even after successful negotiation, parties MAY still send and receive two-party coded text, and both sides must be able to receive it. An answer MUST NOT accept more than one multiparty method in the same RTP session. A session can be modified later by adding or removing the attribute, and after removal the parties MUST NOT send multiparty-formatted text.

A sender uses the multiparty format only when negotiation succeeded and it is conveying text from another source. A mixer that declared the attribute but faces a partner that did not negotiate it SHOULD use the procedure for multiparty-unaware endpoints.
sections.eli5: Before using the name-tag system, both sides say 'I can do name tags'. If one side does not, the helper uses the simple backup way.

sections.title: How the Mixer Fills RTP Packets
sections.content:
Packets keep the RFC 4103 format. In a multiparty session a mixer sets the CC field to 1 and puts exactly one member in the CSRC list: the SSRC of the source of the T140blocks in the packet. Endpoints, and mixers sending their own data, set CC to 0, meaning the source is the SSRC field.

Text from different sources MUST NOT share a packet. New text and redundant copies from the same source go in one packet. The recommended redundancy is one primary and two redundant generations, and a primary or redundant block that is empty is still represented in the redundancy header. Timestamp offsets in that header are relative to the packet's RTP timestamp.

The CSRC list names only the participant whose text is in the packet, not everyone in the conference, since participants who do not type are silent. A mixer also sends RTCP reports with SDES, CNAME and NAME so receivers can build a label for each source, with privacy care because these fields may be sensitive.
sections.eli5: Every bundle of typing gets exactly one name tag, and bundles from different people never share an envelope.

sections.title: Timing, Redundancy and Rate Limits
sections.content:
A mixer sends packets as long as there is new or redundant text. The maximum interval between transmissions from the same source is 330 ms. It is RECOMMENDED to send the next packet as soon as new text is available, as long as the mean character rate over the last 10 one-second intervals stays below the receiver's cps value. The 330 ms figure fits sources that send new text every 300 ms while the user types; it mainly times redundant retransmissions.

The cps default from RFC 4103 is 30 characters per second, evaluated across all sources contributing to a receiver. Endpoints SHOULD declare a higher value; 90 is RECOMMENDED and is judged enough even for large unmanaged conferences and speech-to-text. When the limit is reached, only as much text as fits is sent per interval, and text is divided only at T140block borders.

Text received from a participant SHOULD NOT be sent back to that participant, and when nothing is left to send, transmission stops until new text arrives or a keep-alive is due (RFC 6263 is RECOMMENDED). A BOM character is sent first to open ports and firewalls. If overload builds a delay above 15 seconds, the mixer is RECOMMENDED to discard text and insert a possible-loss indication.
sections.eli5: The helper passes on typing right away, and repeats it a little later in case it got lost. If someone types too fast, the helper hands it over in smaller pieces so nothing jams.

sections.title: Receiving, Recovery and Text Loss
sections.content:
A receiver takes the source from the CSRC list if present, otherwise from the SSRC. It keeps a receive buffer per source. For a packet that is not the first from a source, it works from the oldest redundant generation: the redundant block's timestamp is the packet's RTP timestamp minus its offset, and the block is kept only if that timestamp is later than the latest data already retrieved from that source. The primary block is handled last, with the same test.

Receivers watch RTP sequence numbers for gaps. With one active source, a gap at least as large as the agreed number of redundancy generations (including the primary) probably means lost text. With several active sources it is harder to tell. The RFC offers a simple rule: if three or more packets are lost within one second, insert a possible-text-loss marker. Implementations should prefer marking loss to missing it. Any BOM characters are deleted after extraction.
sections.eli5: Each copy of a message says how old it is. The receiver checks whether it already has that bit and only keeps what is new, and puts a warning mark where something may have gone missing.

sections.title: Fallback for Multiparty-Unaware Endpoints
sections.content:
When the mixer cannot use the multiparty method with a recipient, it SHOULD still make a best-effort single stream by inserting text and labels. It sends text from only one source at a time, adds a Line Separator if the previous text did not end in a new line, and sends a label built from RTCP CNAME and NAME (for example in [ ]) after each source switch.

Suitable switch points include a completed phrase ending with a comma, a completed sentence, a new line, or a long pause (for example more than 10 seconds). If others have waited a long time (for example more than 1 minute), the mixer MAY force a switch at the next word delimiter. The mixer tracks a display count and the last SGR (graphic rendition) code for each source, and replaces backspaces that would erase the label with the letter X.

The limits are real: text from only one source shows at a time, delay varies, erasure only works back to the last switch, and a lost label can cause confusion over who wrote what. The RFC therefore strongly RECOMMENDS building multiparty awareness into endpoints.
sections.eli5: For old devices that cannot read name tags, the helper writes the name in the text itself and lets one person talk at a time, switching at natural pauses.

sections.title: Security and Privacy
sections.content:
The mixer must decrypt, repack and re-encrypt secured text, so it has to be trusted with confidentiality and integrity, as with audio and video mixers. Security SHOULD be applied where possible: SIP over TLS for signalling and DTLS-SRTP (RFC 5764) for media.

RTCP names and addresses may be sensitive, and the RFC notes that users of real-time text services may be deaf or hard of hearing and may not want that revealed. Malicious participants might flood the session, imitate others, or send malformed control codes; receivers MUST keep sources well separated so such effects stay with the offending source. Countermeasures include secure signalling and media, authentication, and blocking, muting or expelling participants.
sections.eli5: The helper in the middle sees everyone's words, so it has to be trustworthy, and names should be shared carefully.
